headline: One pass, right before the exam. If you only remember one thing: the model decides, the harness executes — guardrails are code, not prompt wording.
core_model: Loop: context assembly → model call → decision (end_turn / tool_use) → gate check → tool execution → result fed back → repeat until end_turn or exit condition.
Five actors: User/Entry Point → Harness → Model → Claude API → Tool Backends. The harness is the only one that can enforce a hard rule.
A gate is a code-level check before a tool executes (spend limit, permission scope). No system-prompt wording is ever a substitute for one.

must_know: Subagents don't share context automatically — the coordinator must explicitly pass outputs forward.
Parallelize independent subagent calls; keep orchestration centralized (don't let subagents spawn their own subagents).
Reflection: coordinator checks output for gaps and re-delegates before moving on.
Always define an explicit exit condition (resolve or escalate) — never let a loop run to exhaustion with no resolution.
CLAUDE.md = prose the model reads, not enforced config. Hooks = actual enforcement on a lifecycle event.
Split long/conflicting CLAUDE.md files into scoped nested files (500+ lines degrades adherence).
Plan mode earns its cost on complex/risky changes (touches shared code, auth, many files) — not every edit.
Slash commands share a reusable workflow; they don't enforce it. Permissions still apply in headless/CI runs.
Schema validation catches syntax errors, not semantic ones — add an independent semantic check (do totals reconcile).
Retry-with-error-feedback fixes format/transient issues, not systematic gaps (info the source never had).
Enums need an "other" catch-all; nullable fields should stay null rather than be fabricated when info is absent.
Large tool/schema definitions competing with a large document for context can hurt extraction before the window is even full.
Transient errors (timeouts) are retry-safe; permanent/business errors (validation, permission) are not — return distinct types.
Dry-run/preview is a required gate for destructive tools, and the harness must actually show it before real execution.
Tool selection accuracy drops as the tool library grows — fix with discovery tools or per-context scoping, not just better descriptions.
MCP server scope: project (.mcp.json, shared) vs. user (personal/experimental).
Recall degrades well before the context window is technically full — sliding-window truncation loses info, it doesn't compress it.
Persistent facts (identity, safety-critical info) must be extracted and carried forward explicitly.
System prompt adherence drifts over 10-30+ turns — re-anchor or re-inject core instructions periodically.
Balance clarify-vs-act by the cost of guessing wrong for that specific task — there's no universal right amount of questions.

traps: "Strengthen the system prompt" is almost always the wrong fix when the question describes a hard limit being violated — the right fix is a harness-level gate.
"Context window too small" is a common wrong distractor for a missing-data bug that's actually caused by the coordinator never passing the data at all.
A dry-run parameter that exists but isn't enforced (the harness executes anyway) doesn't count as a real gate.
Splitting a code-review prompt by concern (security/API/business logic) fixes the recall-vs-precision tradeoff a single broad reviewer prompt can't.
Headless/CI Claude Code runs still need permission scoping — no human approver doesn't mean no guardrails.
